clinicalPearls: Caused by obligate intracellular protozoa of the genus Leishmania (~20 species), transmitted by phlebotomine sandflies (Phlebotomus in the Old World, Lutzomyia in the New World); syndromes fall into three categories: visceral (VL), cutaneous (CL), and mucosal (ML) (p.1781).

Visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar, Hindi for 'black fever') is caused by the L. donovani complex (L. donovani, L. infantum); classic presentation is abrupt moderate-to-high fever with rigors, progressive massive splenomegaly, moderate hepatomegaly, weight loss/wasting, and skin hyperpigmentation (p.1782-1783).
Lymphadenopathy is common in most VL-endemic regions but is rare on the Indian subcontinent (p.1783).

VL causes pancytopenia from bone marrow dysfunction and reticuloendothelial infiltration: leukopenia and anemia appear early, followed by thrombocytopenia; there is a marked polyclonal increase in serum immunoglobulins (hypergammaglobulinemia) (p.1782-1783).
Fever with neutropenia or pancytopenia in a patient from an endemic region strongly suggests VL; hypergammaglobulinemia in long-standing illness strengthens the diagnosis (p.1784).
Demonstration of amastigotes in tissue aspirate smears is the gold standard for VL: splenic smear sensitivity is >95%, bone marrow 60-85%, lymph node aspirate ~50% (p.1783).
The rK39 rapid immunochromatographic antibody test is used worldwide for VL field diagnosis (sensitivity ~98%, specificity ~90% in immunocompetent individuals; both lower in East Africa) (p.1783).

Cutaneous leishmaniasis: a sandfly bite is followed days-to-weeks later by a papule that becomes a nodule and ulcerates over weeks-to-months, with raised, indurated margins and a usually painless base; most lesions heal spontaneously over 2-15 months, leaving a scar (p.1786).

Mucosal leishmaniasis (espundia) is typically caused by L. (Viannia) braziliensis and is almost entirely confined to the Americas; it presents with nasal stuffiness and bleeding followed by destruction of nasal cartilage, septal perforation, and collapse of the nasal bridge (p.1787-1788).

Post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis (PKDL) develops in 2-50% of patients during or after cure of VL on the Indian subcontinent and in East Africa, presenting as hypopigmented macules, papules, nodules, or diffuse skin infiltration (p.1785).
Visceral leishmaniasis is a recognized cause of secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH); Leishmania is the most common parasite associated with HLH (p.1369-1370).
harrison.pathophysiology: Sandflies inoculate flagellate promastigotes into the skin; neutrophils first take up the organisms, then macrophages and dendritic cells engulf them, and parasites multiply as nonflagellate amastigotes within macrophages, rupturing cells and invading new macrophages. Acquired resistance depends on a T helper 1 (TH1) response driven by IL-12, IFN-gamma, and TNF-alpha; most infected individuals control infection and never develop symptomatic disease. In active VL there is markedly elevated IL-10, which conditions macrophages for parasite survival, downregulates TNF-alpha and nitric oxide, and suppresses antigen presentation, so patients lack a positive leishmanin (Montenegro) skin test. In VL the reticuloendothelial organs (spleen, liver, lymph nodes, tonsils, intestinal submucosa) are heavily parasitized, and bone marrow dysfunction produces pancytopenia. Diffuse cutaneous leishmaniasis reflects an absent cell-mediated/DTH response with high IL-10, TGF-beta, and IL-4, allowing unchecked parasite multiplication (p.1781-1786).
additionalDifferentials: Malaria (VL is easily mistaken for it)
For CL: cutaneous tuberculosis, fungal infections, leprosy, sarcoidosis, and malignant ulcers
additionalInvestigations: Splenic aspirate smear (highest sensitivity >95%, but invasive and potentially dangerous)
rK39 rapid immunochromatographic antibody test (fingerprick blood/serum, result in ~15 min)
ELISA and indirect immunofluorescent antibody test (IFAT)
Qualitative and quantitative (real-time) PCR for leishmanial nucleic acid (allows species identification)
Loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP) of nucleic acids (point-of-care for VL and PKDL)
Slit skin smears, lesion aspirates/biopsies for CL; tissue biopsy plus PCR for ML
redFlags: Massive (hugely enlarged) splenomegaly with fever and pancytopenia in a patient from or returning from an endemic region
Severe anemia, which may cause congestive heart failure
Bleeding (epistaxis, retinal hemorrhages, gastrointestinal bleeding) from thrombocytopenia
Hypoalbuminemia with pedal edema and ascites in advanced illness
HIV co-infection (untreated VL is fatal in 100% of HIV-co-infected patients)
In ML: destruction of nasal cartilage/septal perforation; aspiration pneumonia may be fatal
harrison.prognosis: Untreated visceral leishmaniasis is fatal in most patients, including 100% of those with HIV co-infection. With effective treatment, recovery is quick: defervescence, regression of splenomegaly, weight gain, and hematologic recovery occur within a week, and continued improvement over 12 months suggests cure; a small percentage relapse (usually within 6-12 months) but respond to retreatment. Cutaneous lesions heal spontaneously in most cases (2-15 months), leaving a scar, but may cause permanent scarring and social stigma. Diffuse cutaneous leishmaniasis does not heal spontaneously and is difficult to treat. Mucosal leishmaniasis does not heal spontaneously despite strong TH1/DTH immunity; the more extensive the disease, the worse the prognosis (p.1782-1788).
pitfalls: VL is easily mistaken for malaria and other tropical febrile illnesses; a careful travel history is essential in nonendemic countries.
Antibody detection tests (rK39, ELISA, IFAT) remain positive for years after cure, so they cannot be used to assess cure or detect relapse, and positive serology does not help diagnose PKDL.
In HIV/VL co-infection serodiagnostic tests may be negative in up to 50% of patients, and parasites may be found in unusual sites (e.g., bronchoalveolar lavage fluid, buffy coat).
Splenic aspiration, though most sensitive, is invasive and may be dangerous in untrained hands.
In PKDL, parasites are scanty and skin smear sensitivity is low, especially in hypopigmented macules (parasites are more readily found in nodular lesions).
Patients with active VL and IL-10-mediated suppression do not have a positive leishmanin (Montenegro) skin test.
In ML the strongly positive DTH response fails to distinguish past from present infection.
harrison.severityClassification: Harrison does not give a formal grading system; leishmaniasis is classified clinically by syndrome: visceral leishmaniasis (VL/kala-azar), cutaneous leishmaniasis (CL, with Old World and New World forms, plus leishmaniasis recidivans and diffuse cutaneous leishmaniasis [DCL]), and mucosal leishmaniasis (ML). Post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis (PKDL) is a sequel of VL.
